newsitem.title: PERU: Peru seeks to halve extreme poverty by year 2000.
newsitem.headline: Peru seeks to halve extreme poverty by year 2000.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said Thursday his government aims to halve by the year 2000 the country's level of extreme poverty, which currently grips 19 percent of Peru's 24 million population.
He added that the state would spend $2.7 billion between 1996 and 2000 on social projects aimed at reducing poverty.

"Poverty is the mark, the deepest and most visible scar left to us of the backwardness and underdevelopment that we have fought for centuries," Fujimori said in a speech outlining his social policies.
Often criticized by Peru's opposition for neglecting poverty in favor of debt accords and free-market reforms, Fujimori insisted that solid economic growth was his government's main weapon.
"A healthy and expanding economy is a necessary condition to boost income and fuel social spending aimed at the poorest. Without economic growth, poverty cannot be reduced," he said.
Speaking at a Lima shantytown, Fujimori said state social spending had risen to $158 per inhabitant in 1996 from $12 in 1990 when his government took power.
He also gave a list of latest figures outlining the nation's poverty levels:
-- Total poverty affected 45 percent of Peruvians in 1995, down from 54 percent in 1991.
-- Extreme poverty was 19 percent in 1995, down from 22 percent in 1991.
-- Infant mortality was 48 per 1,000 births in 1996, down from 62 per 1,000 in 1990.
-- Percentage of homes without direct water access was 38 percent in 1995, down from 43 percent in 1990.
-- Percentage of homes without drainage was 33 percent in 1995, down from 38 percent in 1990.
-- Percentage of homes without electricity was 35 percent in 1995, down from 43 percent in 1990.
Non-governmental organisations say poverty levels are much higher in Peru than state figures show. Some put the total poverty figure at around three-quarters of the population.
"The social investment which is needed, and which we will assume, to execute the current anti-poverty strategy, is estimated to cost about $2.7 billion between 1996 and 2000," Fujimori said.
He added that this spending would concentrate on nutrition, family planning, education, health, highways, irrigation and electricity projects.
"We must not let slip the opportunity that Peru has today to regard itself beyond a doubt as an emerging country," he said.
